text.p: Umpire John Hirschbeck Saturday said he forgives Roberto Alomar for spitting in his face and asked "everyone who loves baseball" to join the two men "in reconciling our differences."
Alomar set off a volcano of controversey when he spit in Hirschbeck's face on September 27 in anger over a third-strike call by Hirschbeck and an argument between the two.

There appeared to be almost universal outrage over Alomar's action and almost as much anger over what many people thought was lenient punishment in suspending the Baltimore Orioles' star second baseman for five days at the beginning of next season.
The umpires threatened to walk out on the playoff games but agreed to abide by a court injuntion won by the owners against a strike.

Ironically, Alomar was a star of the Orioles' defeat of the Cleveland Indians in their divisional playoffs, hitting the game-winning home run in the Orioles' 4-3, 12th-inning victory in Cleveland Saturday.
And the day after the spitting incident, Alomar keyed Baltimore's wild-card berth in the division playoffs with a 10th-inning home run.
The Orioles will play the New York Yankees for the American League pennant starting Tuesday.
Hirshbeck was particularly angered by Alomar saying immediately after the incident that the umpire had become bitter after the death of his young son from a rare brain disease.
Through the Orioles, Alomar released a carefully-worded apology that easily could have been written by a corporate lawyer.
Hirschbeck's written statement was released by the American League.

"I am sure that he wishes as much as I do that this incident had never occurred," Hirschbeck said. "I ask that everyone who loves baseball -- umpires and players, fans, unions and owners -- all join us in reconciling our differences and in mutual respect in and for the great game of baseball."
After the Orioles' victory in Cleveland, Alomar said in a news release: "I have apologised to John and his family, and I will do so in person at our earliest convenience.
"I am sure that (John) believes, like I do, that we should put this behind us and go forward," Alomar said.

Hirschbeck said he and his family were grateful for the support of the Major League Umpires Association and for contributions from all over America to Johns Hopkins University for research into the disease, Adreno Leuko Dystrophy, that killed his son and threatens another son.
Alomar said he donated $50,000 to research for the illness.
"I've been going through a lot of tough times," Alomar said after Saturday's game. "I already did what a had to do. I think it was a mistake on my part. I apologised.
"I think any human being makes mistakes in his life," he said. "Now we have to move on. I'm real happy that I came here and helped my team to win."
Acting baseball commissioner Allan "Bud" Selig, in his own statement, thanked Hirschbeck for forgiving Alomar.
